title: Λέων καὶ κάπρος
titleEn: The Lion and the Wild Boar
part: The Lion and the Wild Boar (Chambry 203)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 203. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Θέρους ἐν ὥρᾳ, ὅτε τὸ καῦμα δίψαν ἐμποιεῖ, εἰς μικρὰν πηγὴν λέων καὶ κάπρος ἦλθον πιεῖν.
sentences.tr: Therous en hōrāi, hote to kauma dipsan empoiei, eis mikran pēgēn leōn kai kapros ēlthon piein.
sentences.l: In the season of summer, when the heat produces thirst, to a small spring a lion and a wild boar came to drink.
sentences.n: θέρους is a genitive dependent on ὥρᾳ, 'in the season of summer'. πιεῖν is a bare aorist infinitive of purpose after a verb of motion, a construction the fables use constantly. The spring is small — that one word is the whole quarrel.

sentences.t: Ἤριζον δὲ τίς πρῶτος αὐτῶν πίῃ· ἐκ τούτου δὲ πρὸς φόνον ἀλλήλων διηγέρθησαν.
sentences.tr: Ērizon de tis prōtos autōn piēi· ek toutou de pros phonon allēlōn diēgerthēsan.
sentences.l: And they were quarrelling over which of them should drink first; and from this they were roused up to the slaughter of one another.
sentences.n: πίῃ is a deliberative subjunctive kept inside the indirect question — the very words of the dispute, 'which of us is to drink first?'

sentences.t: Ἄφνω δὲ ἐπιστραφέντες πρὸς τὸ ἀναπνεῦσαι, εἶδον γῦπας ἐκδεχομένους ὃς ἂν αὐτῶν πέσῃ, τοῦτον καταφαγεῖν.
sentences.tr: Aphnō de epistraphentes pros to anapneusai, eidon gypas ekdechomenous hos an autōn pesēi, touton kataphagein.
sentences.l: And suddenly, having turned round to take breath, they saw vultures waiting — whichever of them should fall, to devour that one.
sentences.i: Suddenly, turning round to catch their breath, they saw vultures waiting to make a meal of whichever of them should fall.
sentences.n: πρὸς τό with the infinitive is the articular infinitive of purpose. The Greek states the vultures' object in its own order: the relative clause ὃς ἂν … πέσῃ comes first and is then picked up by τοῦτον, 'whoever falls — him'. ὃς ἄν with the subjunctive is the indefinite relative, 'whichever one it turns out to be'.

sentences.t: Διὰ τοῦτο λύσαντες τὴν ἔχθραν εἶπον· « Κρεῖσσόν ἐστιν ἡμᾶς φίλους γενέσθαι ἢ βρῶμα γυψὶ καὶ κόραξιν. »
sentences.tr: Dia touto lysantes tēn echthran eipon· « Kreisson estin hēmas philous genesthai ē brōma gypsi kai koraxin. »
sentences.l: For this reason, having dissolved their enmity, they said: « It is better for us to become friends than food for vultures and ravens. »
sentences.n: φίλους and βρῶμα are both predicates of the one infinitive γενέσθαι: to become friends, or to become carrion. The datives γυψὶ καὶ κόραξιν name the parties for whom the food would be food.

sentences.t: Ὅτι τὰς πονηρὰς ἔριδας καὶ τὰς φιλονεικίας καλόν ἐστι διαλύειν, ἐπειδὴ πᾶσιν ἐπικίνδυνον τέλος ἄγουσιν.
sentences.tr: Hoti tas ponēras eridas kai tas philoneikias kalon esti dialyein, epeidē pasin epikindynon telos agousin.
sentences.l: That it is a fine thing to break off wicked quarrels and rivalries, since they bring a dangerous end upon all.
sentences.i: The story shows that it is a fine thing to break off wicked quarrels and rivalries, since they bring a dangerous end upon all.
sentences.n: A bare Ὅτι moral: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line. διαλύειν picks up the λύσαντες of the story — the animals do exactly what the moral prescribes. φιλονεικία is love of winning, the appetite for the contest itself.
